articles.title: Stocks plunge as Amazon, Intel and Alphabet fuel a broad tech sell-off
articles.summary: US stocks plunged in the final trading day of the month as earnings from Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) this week rekindled concerns about the amount of money Big Tech is spending on its AI ambitions. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) tumbled 3.3% as a tech-fueled sell-off intensified. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 1%, or over 500 points, while those on the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 2%. Stocks fell for the second day in a row after Amazon and Alphabet posted rare earnings misses , renewing concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. Amazon shares fell 2%, while Alphabet continued to erase market value after its stock suffered its worst day in over 20 years. Intel ( INTC ) also suffered a brutal reaction to its earnings report, dropping 30% in premarket trading after the company's Q4 outlook came up short. One bright spot in the market was ExxonMobil ( XOM ) and Chevron ( CVX ), whose stocks briefly touched record highs after the oil majors reported that their earnings were boosted as refining margins widened amid the war in the Middle East. Pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca ( AZN ) also reported an earnings beat before the opening bell. While earnings remain in focus, oil prices rebounded higher, putting additional pressure on markets. Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ) rose to $113 per barrel, while WTI crude ( CL=F ) reached $104 per barrel. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) prices tumbled more than 5% as crypto assets were rattled following a $6.3 billion hack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance, marking the largest heist of its kind in history. articles.title: ICE agent indicted on aggravated assault charge for allegedly hitting man with car
articles.summary: HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was indicted by a grand jury Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said. The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, according to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, said District Attorney Sean Teare, who announced the indictment at a news conference that included body camera video of the encounter and a recording of Morales calling 911. ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Teare said is contradicted by video. “The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Teare said. Morales, 33, is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown , although other encounters have come under investigation , including a fatal shooting by an ICE officer this summer in Houston. Morales’ attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client didn't commit a crime and he accused Teare of indicting Morales “for political gain.” Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. “Mr. Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, that has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement,” Lindenmuth told The Associated Press. “To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident — the DA’s office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air.” Teare hinted at concerns over Morales' background but would not provide details. Morales, who is charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare. ICE asserted that local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties. “Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE,” the agency said in a statement. The district attorney played Morales' body camera footage Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales' body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone. The video shows Morales making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes. Morales stops the vehicle, then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away. The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain. Morales is heard saying, “He got hit with a car, bro.” It is not clear to whom he is talking. “I was coming in and I hit him with the car,” Morales says. Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Teare. Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question . After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day. ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. Teare’s office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE’s statement. ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years. Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation Teare has said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He has said Morales left the scene before the vehicle could be impounded. In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had “weaponized his vehicle” before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account . ___ Wilder reported from Austin, Texas. Brook reported from New Orleans. ___ Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues. articles.title: 'I'm deeply hurt': Christa Pike speaks after surviving lethal injection
articles.summary: Christa Pike is speaking out publicly for the first time since she survived an execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30. "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," Pike said in her first public statement since the execution attempt, which her legal team shared Friday. "My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul." Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, and spent 30 years on death row. Two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital failed to kill her during the state's execution attempt last month. She was taken to the hospital, where she received lifesaving care. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez , described the situation as a "mess" and said she was left without justice. “I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” Pike said. "I continue to think about my victim's family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured." Pike's legal team described the outcome as "unprecedented" and said it has raised questions about what happens next in her case. "I don't know why I survived that night," Pike added. "I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone." Pike's survival has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year, and the state's top prison official, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, is stepping down at the end of October. Pike's lawyers said the resignation was "justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now. They said the botched execution "reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement issued earlier this month, according to ABC News . Pike has been held at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center since Oct. 10, where she has been behind bars for more than 30 years. She continues to receive medical care in the prison's infirmary. "I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," her statement read. "But healing is not the same as being okay." What was Christa Pike's condition after the botched execution? When Pike arrived at the hospital, her arms were "swollen, burned and blistered," her lawyers wrote in a legal filing on Oct. 2. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream. Her condition was so severe in the following days, after the execution attempt, that it was believed that she may be brain-dead and could be removed from life support the following day, Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said during a press conference on Oct. 7. "On Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking," he said. Spivey added that Pike is feeling "angry and confused" after waking up in the hospital and is still dealing with major physical problems from the failed execution, including a blood clot, pneumonia and swelling that has left her unable to use both of her arms. "Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery," her legal team wrote in a court filing on Oct. 6. Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press that the latest update "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health will not be clear for some time. "She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here." Pike, pictured in 2007, is conscious and speaking in the hospital, according to her legal team. via REUTERS / REUTERS Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, told the BBC that she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking. "They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," she said. "This has never happened before." Dr. Zivot told the BBC that her survival was "unusual," adding, "Most people who get lethal injection die from it. In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa." Seattle University Law Professor Michael Russo told the Associated Press, "There's nobody else in the history of the death penalty in this country who has gone through what she's been through." The incident with Pike comes a handful of months after the botched attempt to execute Tony Carruthers . In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm, but were unable to insert a secondary IV line. What happens next? All executions in Tennessee are paused for now. Pike's lawyers have called for her sentence to be commuted. State officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, and Gov. Lee has not indicated that he plans to intervene in Pike's case. Lee had denied Pike's clemency before the execution attempt. "I think at the very least the governor should commute Ms. Pike's death sentence to a life sentence," attorney Stephen Ferrell told CNN's State of the Union earlier this month. "We don't know what her physical state will be, but it is clear that she has endured a torturous attempt at executing her." Dr. Zivot said it remains unclear how much pentobarbital entered Pike's system, how much remained in her blood after the injection and what effects she could still experience as she recovers. "I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he said. Professor Russo doubted whether the Supreme Court would stop the state from trying again on double jeopardy grounds — the constitutional protection against being tried or punished twice for the same offense — should it decide to do so. He said, "I think what this Supreme Court would say is, her sentence was to die — to be executed — not to suffer an attempt at execution." "We're in uncharted territory," Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told USA Today . "The U.S. Supreme Court has not decided whether a second execution attempt would violate the Constitution since 1947. These are questions that have never needed to be asked before, and no one knows the answers." articles.title: Renewed Iran war after midterms could threaten fragile U.S. gains in Hormuz
articles.summary: The United States is pointing to gains in the Strait of Hormuz, intent on demonstrating that weeks of complex and secretive military operations there have returned oil flows to near prewar levels and chipped away at a key piece of Iranian leverage ahead of a threatened return to all-out war after the U.S. midterm elections next week. An increase in vessel traffic and the small percentage of ships disabled by Iranian strikes are signals "clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway," read a statement this week from U.S. Central Command announcing that Brad Cooper, the head of the command, had visited the strait. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But while U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf have welcomed the operations along with oil industry and shipping firms, serious questions remain about how sustainable they are in the face of escalating Iranian attacks, according to two people with knowledge of the matter and two Western officials based in the region, who like others interviewed for this report spoke on the condition of anonymity to share sensitive information. Also unclear, they said, is whether the U.S. military would be able to maintain the operations in the strait at the same time as resumed heavy strikes on Iranian territory after the U.S. midterm elections, as President Donald Trump has threatened. In addition to increasing the volume of strikes on shipping, Tehran also appears to have adjusted its targeting in recent weeks, increasingly taking aim at engine rooms to disable vessels rather than just damage them, according to one of the people with knowledge of the matter, who is close to the shipping industry. United Nations data shows that two ships have sunk this month as a result of Iranian attacks. The U.S. operations that have enabled the dramatic increase in oil exports are some of the most complex of the war, according to a European security official and the two people with knowledge of the matter. U.S. forces have integrated air defenses, fighter jets, drones and warships to protect vessels in layers as they pass through the waterway, running a harrowing gantlet of Iranian attacks far beyond what ordinary seafarers sign up to face on the job. The European security official likened the operations to creating "a bubble" that moves along the strait as vessels make the transit. Iranian attacks have made this month the most violent in the waterway since the war began. At least 25 ships in the strait have been hit in October, according to data collected by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, a maritime monitoring body affiliated with the British military. But oil exports have also surged during the same period. Figures vary, but maritime analytics firm Kpler found that average daily oil exports reached 14 million barrels for the week ending on Oct. 18, about 80 percent of prewar averages. The rebound has been remarkable: In July, daily averages over a seven-day period were as low as 7 million barrels. U.S. Central Command doesn't release daily averages, but it said that "since summer," oil exports through the strait had reached 1.5 billion barrels. The U.S. Army's elite 82nd Airborne Division leads the mission and runs a joint operations center in the United Arab Emirates, according to one of the people with knowledge of the matter. The UAE Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the country's role in the Hormuz operations. At least 30 ships per day have transited the strait so far this month, according to the two individuals with knowledge of the matter. U.S. Central Command has released little information publicly about efforts to protect shipping in the strait, but it said Sunday that over the past six months, more than 3,000 commercial vessels have transited the waterway. Speaking about his visit to the strait in a social media video Friday, Cooper said he saw a resumption of shipping but no signs of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "When I flew over the strait, I saw dozens of commercial vessels transiting, all types - cargo, crude oil, liquid natural gas," he said. "I didn't see the IRGC out there at all." The resumption of traffic through the strait - which nearly ceased amid the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran - has brought a critical lifeline for U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf as well as the shipping and energy industries. "Everyone wanted this," said the second person with knowledge of the matter, who is in contact with industry leaders and government officials. But that person cautioned that the private sector and U.S. allies in the region view the effort as an imperfect, temporary measure. The two Western officials based in the region said they have heard similar concerns about the operations in the strait. Since U.S. operations ramped up in August, seven seafarers have been killed and 18 injured, according to United Nations data. The risk levels are currently so high that nearly all the vessels willing to make the trip are state owned and operated. Most private companies continue to refuse to use the strait even under U.S. protection, according to the individuals and officials. "The situation is completely unsustainable," said one of the Western officials based in the region. While vessel traffic has increased for oil exports, the official said, few vessels carrying liquefied natural gas have taken the risk. "If one of those gets hit, it's not just an oil spill; it's an explosion," the official said. The fact that Iran has escalated attacks on shipping is itself a demonstration of U.S. successes in the waterway, according to Gregory Brew, an energy and Iran analyst at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy firm. "The U.S. has achieved something pretty considerable, overcoming Iran's closure of the strait earlier this year, but it's not enough," he said, referring to energy prices that have remained high despite increases to traffic. Iran has demonstrated that it doesn't need to completely close the waterway to keep prices high, but the U.S. has found that even partially reopening the strait isn't moving energy markets the desired amount, according to Brew. "As long as it's contested, then Iran is achieving their objective," he said. But Kevin Donegan, a retired vice admiral who served in Bahrain as the commander of the Navy's Fifth Fleet, said he sees the operations differently. Compared with the escort operations of the "tanker wars" in the 1980s, current U.S. operations have a smaller footprint and are more nimble, he said. "During the tanker wars, ships were lining up and being escorted with lots of naval vessels, big convoys," he said. "We'd brute-force them through in groups. That's not what's happening now." Donegan said he couldn't share further details of the operations, but he described them as "a piece of maritime superiority" that can be turned on and off and moved to where vessels are most vulnerable. "Think of it as a moving sanctuary," he said. Every day, the vessels registered to make the crossing assemble off the coast of the United Arab Emirates and are delivered guidelines to follow, including the instruction to turn off the Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders that broadcast the vessel's location with satellite and radio signals. The vessels are then given coordinates marking the safe passageway, with labeled checkpoints denoted by the NATO phonetic alphabet. Once the vessels have exited the strait, they transfer their cargo to privately owned ships in the Gulf of Oman before traveling back to the Persian Gulf to load up again. Because so few vessels are willing to risk Iranian attacks, roughly the same group of vessels is making the trip back and forth from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman. "It's a de facto shadow fleet," said the Western official based in the region, using a term to describe vessels that attempt to evade sanctions on Russian and Iranian oil by switching off AIS and moving oil with ship-to-ship transfers. Donegan, the retired vice admiral, said the operations also appear to be having a secondary function: They are beginning to build the framework of a future regional coalition to counter Iran. He cited support for the operations from the Emirati, Kuwaiti and Iraqi governments. The Trump administration "has to continue to build this coalition of countries saying that what Iran's doing is not acceptable," he said. "The way forward is to get the Iranians to a tipping point." articles.title: Pope Leo casts historic U.S. vote after years of requesting both parties' primary ballots
articles.summary: VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pontiff to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide America's political future as the Trump era slowly comes to an end. The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in the city ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections , citing his long-standing belief in civic participation. Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” as he has done “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said. The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru, where he lived as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years. “The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added. Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship , and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city-state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections. U.S. federal law allows citizens living abroad, even those working for foreign governments, to vote via absentee ballot. Americans working for foreign governments aren’t automatically at risk of forfeiting their U.S. citizenship, though the U.S. State Department says on its website that it may “actively review” the citizenship status of Americans who “serve as a foreign head of state, foreign head of government, or foreign minister.” This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they’re also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin’s retirement. There are no statewide issues on the Illinois ballot. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot, but he has campaigned hard to try to preserve Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his second term. The pope, registered at a New Lenox, Illinois, address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3, said Kim Fladhammer, chief of staff to the Will County clerk, on Friday. The Chicago Sun-Times first reported the request. The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17. It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope's older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal. Prevost's past votes have gone Democratic and Republican Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections. The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections. While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016. The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022. Clashes with Trump Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants, following the Trump administration’s crackdown and mass deportation program. Earlier this year, Trump called Leo “weak” and captive to the “radical left,” kicking off a remarkable back-and-forth public argument that dominated Leo's April trip to Africa. Responding to Trump, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria: “I’m not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for.” The public dispute has subsided in recent months. “We try to let things pass if there are misunderstandings,” the Vatican foreign minister, Archbishop Richard Paul Gallagher, told reporters this week. "With anybody, we would be looking to approach it and say, ‘OK, there may be a misunderstanding, let’s move on and try to rebuild trust and confidence.’” Leo and Trump have not spoken by phone since the pope's May 2025 election. Last week, however, Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the humanitarian crisis in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky. Asked why Trump and Leo haven't spoken, Gallagher said the Holy See has found a capable conduit in the U.S. ambassador to the Holy See, Brian Burch, and hadn't needed to elevate any issue higher. A pope who follows US politics closely Leo has made clear on several occasions that he follows local and national U.S. politics closely and is not afraid to intervene. Recently, Leo reiterated official church teaching declaring the death penalty “inadmissible.” He made the pronouncement in a social media post on the World Day Against the Death Penalty, which came as the U.S. announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad . The plans were later scrapped. In 2025, Leo intervened in a debate over abortion, after Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich announced plans to give a lifetime achievement award to Sen. Durbin. The plans drew objection from some conservative U.S. bishops given the powerful Democratic senator’s support for abortion rights. Leo called for respect for both sides, but he also pointed out the contradiction between people who call themselves “pro-life” but also support the death penalty. Also in 2025, Leo said he was “very disappointed” that his home state of Illinois approved a law allowing medically assisted dying, which is condemned by the Catholic Church. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, in a note commenting on the confirmation of Leo’s midterm vote, urged Catholics to put “our faith before our politics” and uphold human dignity and the common good. “As Catholics and Americans, we are blessed to be able to participate in our nation’s political and public life,” said the conference’s director of public affairs, Chieko Noguchi. “In voting, our Holy Father sets the example that encourages each citizen to exercise their civic responsibility.” ___ Associated Press writers Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee, and Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, contributed to this report. ___ Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. articles.title: House Dems probe State Department's role in Bolsonaro's escape to U.S. from Brazil
articles.summary: House Democrats are probing the State Department’s role in facilitating former Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro’s escape from Brazil to the U.S. amid ongoing criminal investigations into him and his family. A group of House Democrats, including many prominent members of the Foreign Affairs Committee, sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday night with a list of questions about the State Department’s involvement in Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil and the process it underwent to approve a U.S. visa for him as he departed. In the letter, shared first with POLITICO , the Democrats ask Rubio to clarify how the State Department coordinated with other agencies to grant the visa, whether officials were aware of the pending probes against Bolsonaro and the degree to which the State Department and its officials helped Bolsonaro leave Brazil and come to the United States. “The American people and Congress have a legitimate oversight interest in understanding whether U.S. diplomatic and immigration resources were used to facilitate the travel of a foreign political figure under these circumstances,” the lawmakers wrote. “Transparency is particularly important where the reported events implicate a foreign judicial proceeding, sensitive bilateral relations, and the consistent application of U.S. immigration and diplomatic policies.” The letter, led by Reps. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.) and Dina Titus (D-Nev.), was signed by 25 members in total. The State Department did not respond to a request for comment about the letter. Bolsonaro, the scion of a right-wing political dynasty in the South American country with close ties to key Trump administration advisers, is under investigation in Brazil for alleged money laundering. After he lost the second round of the presidential election to incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday, a Brazilian judge ordered that he surrender his passport and remain in Brazilian territory. Instead, he fled the country with his wife and children, traveling first to Argentina and then Miami. POLITICO has not been able to independently confirm those reports. The White House directed a request for comment about administration involvement to the State Department as well as Customs and Border Protection. The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees CBP, did not address reports of administration involvement directly, but did say in a statement that “Bolsonaro arrived in South Florida with his family and were met and inspected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection in accordance with applicable immigration laws and procedures. At the conclusion of the inspection, Mr. Bolsonaro and his accompanying family members were released.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/30/democrats-demand-answers-bolsonaro-01141553
articles.author: Eric Bazail-Eimil

articles.title: 'It could be quite a brutal evening': GOP braces for some once-unthinkable losses
articles.summary: Republicans are bracing for a brutal election night, convinced they're set to face some previously unthinkable losses in deep-red Trump territory as key battleground races hang on a knife's edge . House Republicans are privately discussing not just if they'll lose their majority, but by how many seats. Imperiled GOP incumbents in once safe districts have been begging party leaders for more money in the final few days to stem the bleeding, according to six people involved in internal conversations, granted anonymity to discuss them. Senate Republicans have found new cause to worry about contests in Ohio, Kansas and other red states. "It could be quite a brutal evening," said one senior Republican involved in the private conversations, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. "Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them." Some Republican incumbents made an eyebrow-raising emergency decision. They stopped doing their own polling weeks ago as they tried to save every dollar for swaying voters as they begged for the GOP cavalry to arrive from President Donald Trump's political operation to the National Republican Congressional Committee, according to three of the people. One Republican strategist working on midterm races simply responded to a question about the environment with a video of a dumpster on fire that was being swept away by flood waters. Top GOP officials and lawmakers have long known the political landscape would be bad, amid voter anger over the cost of living and aspects of Trump's policy agenda. But they're facing a worse position than they expected earlier this year, with less than one week until Election Day. Republicans for weeks have worried that young men who'd voted for Trump, including white and Hispanic working class voters, will stay home amid disillusionment with high costs and the Iran war. That alone could allow Democrats to overperform in some areas after they hemorrhaged support among that voting bloc in 2024. At a Kwik Trip in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, this week in the hotly-contested 3rd District, Isaiah Romero was filling up his silver Ram truck. The 20-year-old said he cast his ballot for Trump in his first ever presidential election two years ago. His verdict on high fuel prices? "I think they're bull," he said as he looked over to the $6.39 per gallon diesel and $4.29 gas at the pump. Is he voting this time? "No," Romero responded, adding: "I didn't vote for this." New fires have been popping up across the map just as soon as top GOP officials put out others. Trump canceled in-person rallies in deep-red Kansas and Iowa set for this weekend to instead hold a series of tele-rallies for GOP candidates in the final stretch. "Any Democrats telling you they aren't winning the Senate [besides] a couple of seats are sandbagging expectations," the senior Republican said. In Ohio, the race between GOP Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is still incredibly close in private and public polling. But Republicans have watched with horror as GOP governor nominee "Vivek's [Ramaswamy's] numbers have gone off a cliff" in the last few days after he ran an ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother saying her daughter is a liar, according to the senior Republican and two others who saw the internal polling. Acton's stepfather was charged with raping her when she was 12. The headwinds across all of Ohio are deeply problematic for Republicans. They now believe embattled Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) — who is facing child and domestic abuse allegations that he denies — will lose in a seat Trump won by double digits. South Carolina has become another unexpectedly nailbiting race for Republicans, where political newcomer Sen. Darline Graham is facing a well-funded Democratic challenger. But GOP operatives and officials are feeling somewhat better after outside groups injected cash into the race earlier this month and Trump announced another rally in the state to energize Republicans' base. "It's a lot closer than I think we would ever want, but I think she's going to pull it out," said Jeff Davis, chair of the Greenville County Republican Party. But in one of the most dire signs, once-unimaginable GOP worries have started to creep about deep-red Louisiana — where Trump announced this week he will hold an election-eve tele-rally for Senate nominee Julia Letlow. Speaker Mike Johnson, who is close with Letlow, will join as Republicans have grown wary about a surge of Black voters and other Democratic-leaning voters in early voting across the South. Senior Republicans believe Letlow will win, but they fear it will be by single digits if nothing changes. "The cakewalk turned into a knife fight," said one Louisiana Republican who has talked with Letlow recently. "If Democrat turnout surges on Election Day, it'll be a long night in Monroe," the person added, and they expect Letlow to win by just 6 points in a state Trump won by 22 points two years ago. In another painful development for Republicans in Louisiana, GOP groups have even started an eye-popping spending war in a safe red gerrymandered seat — where a bitter Republican-on-Republican primary is unfolding between state Sen. Blake Miguez, who was formerly endorsed by Trump , and state Sen. Rick Edmonds, Johnson's former pastor. Club for Growth poured another $220,000 into the race Thursday. Republicans fear the messy race is poised for a December runoff. "POLITICO's sad little rolodex of loser strategists have no idea what they're talking about, and if they really believe what they're saying they should come out of the shadows and put a name to their brain-dead comments," said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. "While Republicans have focused on real solutions to improve costs of living and make our nation safer, Democrats have nominated a gang of radicals who want to raise taxes, force everyone on government healthcare, and release criminals onto the streets," said Joanna Rodriguez, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee. On the House side, Republicans are bracing for a brutal night. But they've long been spending in some redder GOP districts to forestall a true disaster. Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, said that the committee worked in partnership with the campaigns and the RNC to launch coordinated advertising early in GOP-held districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (Colo.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Rob Wittman (Va.), Mike Turner (Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (Texas). The NRCC began airing coordinated ads in early August, more than a month before the DCCC. The NRCC also conducted polling in more than 100 districts, an eye-popping number, as they worked to see how far the fires had spread into red terrain and make sure they were moving resources where they were needed. Republicans still think they can unseat Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), while flipping retiring Rep. Jared Golden's (D-Maine) seat. But privately, Republicans believe North Carolina's open 11th District is close to gone, as are several other deep-red seats Trump won by double digits, according to four people with knowledge of the situation. And they're still not confident they'll beat Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) in a seat the GOP thought would be an easy flip when they redrew it early this year. It's become the most expensive House race in history. The Republican in Kentucky's 6th district, where Trump won by 15 points in 2024, is barely hanging on, according to the four people. Even in the South Texas districts the GOP redrew in their favor, Republicans reached the point days ago where no amount of new money is going to change the upcoming catastrophe, said one Republican official involved in conversations about those races. Johnson traveled to Minnesota on Thursday to headline a fundraiser for GOP Rep. Brad Finstad, who Republicans are scrambling to shore up in a +12 Trump district. Finstad told POLITICO in an interview this week that he had warned senior Republicans for weeks about Democratic groups pouring money into the race in his southern Minnesota district. "We raised that with anybody and everybody that would want to hear it," Finstad said. "From a global perspective, people were like, 'Well, you won by 18, you're fine.' And, you know, those of us in Minnesota know that this district has always had kind of an independent streak to it." Senate Democrats, meanwhile, are upbeat at their prospects, but public and private polling across close to the entire battleground map is running within the margin of error — meaning those states could break either way. "I would rather be us than them. But if anyone tells you they know what's going to happen, they're full of shit," one senior Senate Democratic operative said. "Everything is close." And some Republicans are taking solace in the fact that at least it'll all soon be over. "I can see the light at the end of the tunnel," said a GOP strategist working on a campaign that is trending toward Democrats. "It might be a semi-truck, but at least I can see it." Andrew Howard, Erin Doherty and Alec Hernández contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/could-quite-brutal-evening-gop-090000456.html

articles.title: Pentagon reportedly tells NATO allies to tone down rhetoric about Russia
articles.summary: By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pentagon officials have in recent weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said. Among the nations that have received ‌messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. It was not clear if the messages, ‌which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments. The US requests come as the Trump administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The ​latest push has blended incentives for Russia - including sanctions relief - with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations." Among the comments that have drawn US officials' attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said. ‌Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved. None of the people, ⁠who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner. EUROPE SHOULD AVOID "POKING" RUSSIA The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia. Some Western officials have argued that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play ⁠into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine. Others argue European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent. Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign. One of the people familiar told Reuters that Colby told a ​Baltic ​official recently that there should be no "poking" directed at the Russians. The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting ​that Russia was "cornered like a rat" as an example of unhelpful rhetoric. It was ‌not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a "rat in a corner" in late September, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine. "We are helping you. The Americans are there," said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon's recent private messaging. "Just don't be loud. Don't make noise." In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be "measured" in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement. The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment. MOSCOW TESTS EUROPE'S RESOLVE One of the European officials said that the Pentagon's advice, ‌while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down ​the probability of Russia testing NATO's mutual defense provisions. Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could ​dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future. The Pentagon messages to NATO officials ​come at a fraught time for European security. Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said. On Wednesday, German prosecutors ‌said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a ​building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg ​area. In September, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied. At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration's push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin's continued ​economic isolation. Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington's force posture in Europe, a ‌process that could see a sharp drawdown in America's troop presence on the continent. US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, ​particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia. (Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski in New York, Gram Slattery in Washington and Andrius ​Sytas in Vilnius; Additional reporting by Phil Stewart in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/exclusive-pentagon-tells-europeans-cool-050400616.html
articles.author: By Antoni Slodkowski, Gram Slattery and Andrius Sytas

articles.title: U.S. scraps G20 group photo after European diplomats refuse to pose with Russia's Lavrov
articles.summary: ATLANTA (AP) — The top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies opened two days of meetings in Atlanta on Friday after European objections to Russia’s participation forced the U.S. to cancel a photo of the foreign ministers, underscoring deep rifts among the group over global crises . Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug on the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that usually helps kick off such diplomatic gatherings. But he still opened the talks, which otherwise went ahead as planned, with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade. “We are in a critical moment — I would call it a moment of choosing, and I would say not just for my country, the United States of America, but frankly, for the world," Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises,” he added, pointing to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation. Many are posing “severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order.” Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they face. Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran , U.S. tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea . All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade. Russia's presence at G20 gathering roils European allies Concerns about any prospects for the talks escalated when the Europeans balked at being photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Rubio decided to scrap the picture because he thought the controversy would be a distraction, according to two U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter. Some G20 countries had already expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance. The British foreign office said in a statement that the United Kingdom “has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that.” Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said the cancellation of the group photo was “the right decision” by the U.S., telling media in Atlanta that “I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov.” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said “there is no normality with Russia” but “we must exchange the controversies at the table here,” the German news agency dpa reported. He added that “we also must not send falsely optimistic signals.” Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. His presence in Atlanta could cause domestic political problems for Trump just days before the U.S. congressional midterm elections as well as roil the G20, according to Ian Kelly, a U.S. ambassador to Georgia during Trump’s first term. “It seems politically boneheaded to invite him,” said Kelly, who now teaches international relations and diplomacy at Northwestern University outside Chicago. The meeting in Atlanta is meant to set the stage for a G20 leaders’ summit hosted by President Donald Trump at his Miami golf club in December. It is unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump’s invitation to that gathering. G20 member South Africa was not invited Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as U.S. officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group. But missing from the invite list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top U.S. officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted. “We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola. Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate “on an equal footing with other members” when Britain takes over the presidency next year. The Iran war hangs over the G20 event The U.S. has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz , the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea. The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors. But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections and the possibility that Iran will retaliate against them. ___ Associated Press writers Michelle Gumede in Johannesburg, South Africa, Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, Geir Moulson in Berlin, Jill Lawless in London and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/g20-diplomats-including-china-russia-040255027.html

articles.title: DOJ subpoenas California election officials in ballooning voter fraud probe
articles.summary: Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, stands after holding a Justice Department news conference on Aug. 13, 2026. (Allen J. Schaben/TNS) The Department of Justice has subpoenaed local election officials in at least four California counties, the latest development in its unprecedented effort to usurp the state's authority and prove allegations of widespread voter fraud in the runup to the midterm election. The Chronicle obtained subpoenas sent to election officials in Los Angeles and Orange  counties seeking possible instances of noncitizen voting and unredacted information about certain voters, including their registration, address, voting history and citizenship status. Santa Clara County confirmed it had also received subpoenas and inewsource reported that San Diego County officials received them as well. The subpoenas were sent as part of criminal investigations into alleged fraudulent voting by noncitizens. For more election coverage from the San Francisco Chronicle One of the subpoenas was received as recently as Oct. 29. Others were sent in September. The subpoenas reviewed by the Chronicle were sent before a federal judge in a separate case gave a stern warning to First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, who has spearheaded the agency's attempts to force California to surrender its authority to administer its own elections, to stop threatening local election officials. At a hearing on Tuesday, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter told Essayli: "This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately."  He repeated the message in a ruling Wednesday denying Essayli's attempt to force California to sequester 20,000 ballots the DOJ has said could have been sent to noncitizens. "The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop," Carter wrote. The subpoenas do not mean that the election officials who received them are themselves under investigation. But the DOJ has separately threatened many of the same officials by giving them 48 hours to review lists of alleged noncitizen voters, and threatening them with criminal prosecution if they do not comply. Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan said Carter's warning was timely, and important. His office was at the center of the Trump administration's unsuccessful effort to sequester 20,000 ballots. "Judge Carter's admonishment about threats directed at election officials on Tuesday was well placed and appreciated," he said in a statement. "At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law. Clear court rulings at both the U.S. District Court level and the Court of Appeals have confirmed that. Threats and intimidation have no place in elections. We will take whatever steps necessary to ensure the safety of our employees and to remain focused on serving the voters of Los Angeles County so they can exercise their voting franchise." His office received three federal grand jury subpoenas last week from Essayli and agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the unit the Trump administration has tasked with leading criminal investigations into suspected voter fraud. The subpoenas ask individual election officials to turn over any information that "tends to indicate an alien has voted in a federal election" and that indicates "someone has aided and/or abetted an alien voting in a federal election." The subpoenas also cast a wide net for any communications regarding the back-and-forth between the Justice Department and California secretary of state's office about the administration's downgraded claims of fraud in the state. After initially claiming more than 190,000 noncitizens were potentially registered in California, the federal government went silent for three months before claiming that 20,000 were improperly registered. Federal prosecutors then charged only 28 California residents with citizen-related voter fraud, five of whom are not accused of voting. The subpoenas also seek the registrar's office's methods for preventing voting by noncitizens. The most recent subpoena to Orange County, sent Oct. 23 and received Thursday, according to a date stamp, asks for the unredacted voter records for some 60 individuals from January 2017 through the present. In L.A. County, officials were directed to appear with the requested materials at the federal courthouse in Santa Ana on Nov. 4, one day after the election. In Orange County, the appearance date is Nov. 18. In total, Orange County has been hit with four subpoenas requesting unredacted voter registration information for a total of 80 possible registrants, though Registrar Bob Page noted there has been overlap in the names the federal government has provided. The county also received three subpoenas in September requesting unredacted voter registration material. Page said his office had complied with them. "The Registrar of Voters provided responsive documents requested in the three September subpoenas," he said in an email. "We plan to provide responsive documents for the subpoena delivered to us today." A spokesperson for Santa Clara County said its registrar of voters received two federal subpoenas in September, but did not immediately provide copies. Carter said in his Wednesday ruling that taken together, the DOJ's actions in California represent "a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials." Election law experts quickly condemned news of the subpoenas. "These efforts must be called what they are: a blatant attempt by a politicized and weaponized Justice Department to serve a desperate president's political agenda," Center for Election Innovation and Research Executive Director David Becker, a former DOJ attorney, said in a statement. Citing Carter's demand that federal officials cease threatening local election workers, Becker added, "In response, the DOJ has doubled down."
